_note: Watershed rebuild parameters (docs/water/watershed_rebuild_design.md). One file for every stage, so a run is reproduced from it and the input hashes in its manifest.

uplift._note: Stage A2: where and how fast the land rose (m/yr): high where the landform is high, from the landform smoothed at smooth_m, so it varies only at the scale of the massifs. Nothing is added at hill scale. Sonny 7 Nov: the first R1 run's plane-wave variation (2.4 and 1.1 km) showed as regular blobs, an arbitrary pattern the watershed document rules out (section 11: variety from conditions, not randomisation). Hill-scale variety comes from the folded rock bands (hard and soft beds), the rain and the drainage itself.
uplift._calibration_note: Sonny 7 Nov, after run c3b1b846 (35 degree slope limit): the summit fell to 835 m (landform 1,459 m) while the mean land rose to 190 m (landform 155 m). The massif centres were cut about 400 m and their flanks rose, because the uplift is flat-topped (clipped at ref_height_m) and broad, and the eroded island's heights follow drainage distance, not the landform's peaks. One scalar cannot fix both, so evolve.py --calibrate=PREV_RUN_DIR scales the uplift by (landform + offset) / (previous result + offset), both smoothed at smooth_m (massif scale only; no hill-scale pattern). Relief scales with U at steady state, so one pass should bring both the summit and the mean near the landform. The summary's massif_scale_height_mismatch_m says how close it is.

rain._note: Stage A4: Smith and Barstad (2004) linear orographic rain on a coarse grid, smoothed up to the model grid; wind direction per tile row from the landform manifest (climate.wind_toward_x). The linear theory gives the rate WHILE moist air is lifted, not an annual total. Annual rain = max(background + storm_share x orographic rate, min_share x background): all background rain is taken to fall in the moist onshore spells, and lee slopes keep at least min_share of it from other weather. storm_share is calibrated once against a real maritime peak (calibration_peak): the first R1 run (storm rate used all year) peaked at 13,300 mm/yr on the middle massif's west flank; 0.25 brings that peak to about 4,100 mm/yr. It is a climate property (share of the year with moist onshore flow), so it stays fixed if the landform changes.
rain.calibration_peak: Ben Nevis summit observatory, 1,345 m, west Scotland, mean 4,104 mm/yr over 1883-1904 (Wikipedia climate table, checked 7 Nov 2026)

rock._note: Stage A3: rock ids from the geology export (export_geology.gd --step equal to the model cell). soluble: carbonate rock that water dissolves (karst: sinkholes, sinking streams, springs, dry valleys). cave_forming: the soluble rocks strong enough to hold open caves; chalk is soluble but weak and porous, so it gives dry valleys, bournes and springs at its base, rarely caves. Fractured basalt (lava tubes) and fault zones can also feed cave springs (stage C7); they come from the geology features, not from this list.

water_budget._note: Stage A5 (runoff.py), the one water budget used by the erosion (R2) and the hydrology (R3 to R5). pet_mm_yr: Penman potential evaporation, MORECS average for Scotland 1961-93, 483 +/- 31.5 mm/yr (Institute of Hydrology report, NORA 15503); the same report finds little change with height in such uplands, so it is not lapsed with height. fu_omega: Fu's Budyko parameter; 2.6 is the value usually quoted as matching Budyko's original curve (Zhang et al. 2004). In our wet climate (rain about 1,700 mm against 483) ET stays near PET: for omega 2 to 3.5, ET at 1,665 mm of rain is 414 to 476 mm. Forest interception (700 to 1,200 mm in the same report) comes later, when the vegetation reads the record. bfi_by_rock: base flow index by rock, midpoints of the UK Low Flow Studies report 3 (Institute of Hydrology 1980), table 3.3: chalk 0.90-0.98; Carboniferous limestone 0.20-0.75 (karst conduits make it flashy); coal measures 0.40-0.55; Silurian and Ordovician metamorphic and igneous rocks 0.30-0.50; Oxford Clay (a mudstone) 0.30-0.50; Old Red Sandstone 0.45-0.55 (our sandstone lies in a folded sequence with slate and marble, so a compacted old sandstone is the analogue, not the porous Permo-Triassic 0.70-0.80). By analogy, flagged for the R4 research pass: marble as limestone; slate, granite, basalt and tuff as the metamorphic and igneous class (young jointed basalt can be far more permeable). sediment (loose superficial deposits in the rock table): 0.56, the superficial diamicton of Bloomfield, Bricker and Newell (2011, Thames basin, table II), whose values for the solid rocks agree with the table above (chalk 0.95, oolitic limestone 0.85, Gault and London Clay mudstones 0.35 and 0.36). reference_bfi: the impermeable class, the unit of the erosion's discharge.

evolve._note: Stage B (evolve.py). K, m and D follow the earlier pre-carve runs (tools/erosion_precarve real_run: K 4e-6, m 0.5, D 0.05 m2/yr). G is the dimensionless deposition coefficient (about 1: deposition matters, floodplains and fans form). channel_head: where channels begin (slope-area rule, below). Not yet tuned on our island: R2's first run sets them. start_roughness_m: uncorrelated starting roughness (fixed by world position) so channels branch instead of running in parallel lines; erosion removes it. years and dt (Sonny 7 Nov, after Dino's stable 1 Myr run): in 1 Myr the summit still rose 0.8 m/kyr, almost the full uplift (0.96), because the erosion had not yet climbed to the tops (a knickpoint moves at about K Q^m, a few m/kyr in small catchments). 4 Myr in 250 steps of 16 kyr costs the same run time; the implicit fluvial step is stable at any dt and creep takes its own sub-steps. The summary's last_tenth_* numbers say whether steady state was reached. Relief at steady state scales with U/K, so uplift.base_m_per_yr is then calibrated once so the final summit matches the landform's. K and D x3 (Sonny 7 Nov, after the 4 Myr run 58ecf498): the summit reached 3,521 m and was still rising 0.35 m/kyr (mean land 155 to 541 m), so uplift outran erosion. Steady-state relief scales with U/K and the time to reach it with 1/K, so raising K three times lowers the relief about three times and brings steady state three times sooner. D rises with K so D/K, which sets valley spacing (Perron et al. 2009), is unchanged. Creep is now implicit, so a larger D costs no sub-steps.
evolve._dissection_note: Sonny 8 Nov, after run 506dadff: the massif-scale calibration matched (mean mismatch 9 m, 5th to 95th percentile -54 to +48 m), yet the summit was 894 m against the landform's 1,459 m and the massif centres were cut about 400 m. A steady state keeps the landform only at the smoothing scale: with threshold slopes and the valley spacing set by D/K, no ridge stands more than a couple of hundred metres above its valleys, so a peaked massif becomes an evenly dissected one. Islands like this one (Arran, Skye, the Highlands) are not in steady state: they are uplifted older surfaces that rivers and then ice are still cutting into, with summit plateaus between deep glens. So B1 now dissects the landform as it stands: uplift_share 0 (the landform is the land as uplifted), and the run length is chosen from snapshots (snapshot_years, each written to OUT_DIR/t<kyr>k with its own summary and picture) by the checks: summits near the landform's, the main valleys reaching into the massif cores, and the drainage and slope figures. Knickpoints climb at about K A^m (tens of km per Myr for 10 km2 catchments at this K), so 0.25 to 2 Myr spans young to deeply dissected. dt 2,500 years (since 8 Nov, for the fast early dissection) so every snapshot falls on a step. The by-rock threshold (threshold_slope_deg_by_rock) lets hard-rock peaks stand as steep walls instead of being cut back to 35 degrees.
evolve._creep_and_peaks_note: Sonny 8 Nov, after run 11bbbcc9 (dissection, no uplift, D 0.15): the island wore down to a low plain (summit 680 m at 0.25 Myr, 167 m at 2 Myr; drainage density 15 to 0.8 km/km2), and the summit fell 200 m in the first 5 kyr step. D 0.15 m2/yr was set only to keep D/K while K was raised for a quick steady state; it is 30 to 50 times measured soil creep and it rounded the peaks away. Roering, Kirchner and Dietrich (1999, WRR 35(3):853-870, checked 8 Nov) measured 0.0032 +- 0.0009 m2/yr in the Oregon Coast Range (0.0031 to 0.0045 over five basins), with a critical gradient of 1.25 (51 degrees) for soil-mantled slopes, so the by-rock thresholds above sit inside the measured range. Here the valley spacing comes from the channel-head rule, not from D/K, so D goes back to a measured value: 0.005 m2/yr, the top of that range, for a wetter, frost-active climate. Bare hard-rock peaks are not soil-mantled at all, and creep already runs at D * ery^0.3. The dissection front moves fast at this K in soft rock (a knickpoint at K e Q^m: about 60 km/Myr for 10 km2 of tuff or shale, 3 km/Myr of granite), so the run is 0.5 Myr with snapshots from 25 kyr. The summary's landform_peaks (the summit rule: valleys carved, peaks kept at the landform's heights) and height_change_by_process (river and slides against creep, at the peaks and over all land) say which process sets the peaks.
evolve._incision_threshold_note: Sonny 8 Nov, after run d9f89615 (measured creep): creep moved 1 to 6 m near the peaks, rivers and slides 63 to 768 m, and every landform peak lost over 100 m by 0.15 Myr, while valleys cut up to 338 m in the first 25 kyr. A channel cuts bedrock only where its flow can move the boulders and gravel on its bed, so erosion is K e (Q^m S - incision_threshold_m), never below 0, on bedrock (none on loose sediment over 1 m). With m 0.5 and Q close to the drainage area, Q^m S is the channel steepness index: in the San Gabriel Mountains catchment erosion rises from 35 m/Myr at the lowest steepness to 1,100 m/Myr, non-linearly, which a threshold incision model explains (DiBiase et al. 2010, EPSL 289:134; DiBiase and Whipple 2011, JGR 116:F04036, critical shear stress 45 Pa for 90 mm gravel). 30 m is a judged value near the low end of their steepness range (to check on the maps): a 1 ha hollow at slope 0.3 does not cut, a 1 km2 valley at 0.1 cuts at 70% of the full rate, a 10 km2 valley at 0.05 at 80%. This is the document's 'no deep gullies under tiny flows'.
evolve._threshold_note: Threshold hillslopes (Sonny 7 Nov, after run 624bd23c grew a south-east ridge more than 1,000 m above its landform with 40 to 45 degree flanks, still rising 0.2 m/kyr). Linear creep has no slope limit, so where uplift beats the rivers a ridge steepens without end. Real hillslopes fail by landslides past a threshold angle and keep a mean angle near it whatever the erosion rate: Burbank et al. 1996 (Nature 379:505) found steep hillslope angles essentially independent of erosion rate; Montgomery 2001 (Am. J. Sci. 301:432) reads the same limit from slope distributions. The angle lies between the angle of repose of loose debris (about 33 degrees) and the steeper limit soil-mantled slopes hold (Roering et al. 1999, Water Resources Research 35:853, fit a critical slope of 1.25, about 51 degrees, in the Oregon Coast Range). 35 degrees (tangent 0.70) is taken as the mean over a 16 m cell; crags and rock steps steeper than that inside a cell are fine detail for later stages. The run's slope shares check it. A by-rock value (hard rock holds steeper walls: Schmidt and Montgomery 1995, Science 270:617) is the next refinement, with sources, in R2b, where glacial cirque walls and trough sides need it. 0 turns the limit off.
evolve._threshold_by_rock_note: Sonny 8 Nov, after Dave asked for tall, epic, fantasy-scale peaks (8 Nov 01:19). Hard rock holds steeper walls than soft rock: relief is limited by rock mass strength (Schmidt and Montgomery 1995, Science 270:617), and real hard-rock mountain walls (gabbro and basalt in the Skye Cuillin, rhyolite and andesite in Glen Coe) stand well above 35 degrees over tens of metres. These values are the art goal's light fantasy exaggeration within that real range: granite and basalt 48, slate and marble 44, limestone 42, sandstone 40, tuff 38; shale, coal, chalk and loose sediment keep 35 (threshold_slope_deg, also used under loose cover over 1 m). Not from a measured table: judged on the maps.

channel_head._note: A channel begins where Q * S^slope_exponent passes area_m2_at_ref_slope * ref_slope^slope_exponent (Q the quick-runoff-weighted area, S the slope to the receiver) and then runs on downstream at any slope. Montgomery and Dietrich (1988): the source area of a channel head falls as slope rises (about as S^-2) and is larger in drier ground. 2 ha at a slope of 0.15 means about 0.3 ha at 0.4 and 4.5 ha at 0.1. Not yet tuned on our island.

glacial._note: Stage B2 (glacial.py, step R2b): one cold stage after the B1 river era, then the post-glacial era. Model: Hergarten 2021 (Earth Surface Dynamics 9:937), glacial stream power with a swath and finite ice thickness; benchmarked against iSOSIA by Liebl et al. 2023 (GMD 16:1315). From the paper: full_ice_above_ela_m 500 (his examples: H_f - H_e = 2 units of 250 m); glacial_K_ratio 2 (his fluvioglacial runs, K_g = 2 K); width w = width_m_at_ref_flux * (A_i / ref_flux_m2)^0.3 (eq. 13; his examples set w = A_i^0.3 in grid units with 50 m cells, so 50 m at 2,500 m2; that gives about 1.3 km for a 120 km2 ice catchment); thickness_to_width 0.25 (his delta 0.05 in units of 250 m vertical over 50 m horizontal); swath_eps 0.25 (eq. 22, used in all his runs); ice_carry_ratio 10 (section 5 says the glacier carries sediment 10 times more efficiently than water; the K_t values printed there were not legible in the cloud copy, to check against the PDF). Not from a source yet, judged on the maps: ela_m 487 is the design's start, the reconstructed Loch Lomond Stadial equilibrium line at Coire Breac (eastern Grampians); years 100,000 is the time the island spends under stadial-sized ice, a stand-in for many Pleistocene cold stages (checked against trough overdeepening of 100 to 300 m and cirque floors in the result); cold_pet_mm_yr 250 is a guess at a stadial PET (about half of today's 483). Frozen ground: all cold-stage runoff is quick (permafrost made chalk impervious, the classic dry-valley explanation; Goudie 1990, p. 176). post_glacial_years 11,700: the Holocene. scour_m: a hollow whose floor the ice lowered more than this counts as ice-scoured (R3 names it a rock basin, or a cirque when it lies high).
